title: Digitalretailing
content:
1. It's a snowy Saturday in Chicago, but Amy, age 28, needs resort-wear for a vacation. Five years ago, she would have headed straight for the mall. Today she starts shopping by launching a video conversation with a retailer at Danella, where she bought two outfits the previous month. The retailer recommends several items, superimposing photos of them onto Amy's image. Amy rejects a couple of items immediately. After researching customer reviews and prices, she finds better deals on several items at another retailer, and orders them. She buys one item from Danella online and then drives to the Danella store near her for the in-stock items she wants to try on.

2. As Amy enters Danella, a sales associate greets her by name and walks her to a dressing room stocked with her online selections – plus some matching shoes. She likes the shoes, so she scans the bar code into her smartphone and finds the same pair for $30 less at another store. The sales associate quickly offers to match the price, and encourages Amy to try on the dress. It is daring and expensive, so Amy sends a video to three friends, asking for their opinion. The responses come quickly: three thumbs-down. She collects the items she wants, scans an Internet site for coupons (saving an additional $73), and checks out with her smartphone.

3. As she heads for the door, a life-size screen recognizes her and shows a special offer on an irresistible summer-weight top. Amy checks her budget online, smiles, and uses her phone to scan the QR code on the screen. The item will be shipped to her home the next day.

4. This is just a story, but it's not as fanciful as you might think. All the technology Amy uses is already available – and within five years, much of it will be available everywhere. But what seems like a dream come true for the shopper – a wealth of information, near-perfect price transparency, a lot of special deals – is already feeling more like a nightmare for many retailers.

5. Why will digital retailing continue to grow so fast? Why won't it peak sometime soon? Anyone who has shopped online knows at least part of the answer. The selection is huge yet very easy to search. The prices are good and easily compared. It's convenient: You can do it at home or at work, without using gasoline or fighting to park. Half of online purchases are delivered free to US consumers. Many returns are free as well. Product reviews and recommendations are extensive. Little wonder that the average American Customer Satisfaction Index score for online retailers such as Amazon is higher than the average for physical discount and department stores.

6. The advantages of digital retailing are increasing as innovations flood the market. For instance, Amazon has already earned valuable patents on key innovations such as 1-Click checkout and an online system that allows consumers to exchange unwanted gifts even before receiving them. Digital retailers drive innovation by spending heavily on recruiting, wages, and bonuses to attract and retain top technical talent. They were also among the first to use cloud computing and to enhance marketing efficiency through social networks and online advertising.
